reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A group of ciliopathies defined by malformations of the oral cavity, face, and digits, with several distinct subtypes differing in inheritance and associated features
Oral findings include lobulated or bifid tongue with hamartomas, multiple frenula, cleft palate or lip, and dental anomalies
Facial features may include hypertelorism, a broad or bifid nasal tip, and micrognathia, while digital anomalies include brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly, and polydactyly
Type I is X-linked dominant, caused by OFD1 variants and typically lethal in males, and is frequently associated with polycystic kidney disease and central nervous system malformation
Central nervous system involvement can include agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar and posterior fossa anomalies including the molar tooth sign, and intracerebral cysts
As a ciliopathy it overlaps with Joubert syndrome and other disorders, and the OFD1 gene product localises to the centriole and basal body of the primary cilium
Diagnosis integrates the oral-facial-digital pattern with imaging of brain and kidneys and molecular confirmation for subtype classification and counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Oral-facial-digital syndromes are ciliopathies in which defective primary cilium and basal body function disrupts developmental signalling that patterns midline craniofacial structures, the palate and tongue, and the limbs. The prototypic type I results from variants in OFD1, encoding a centriolar and basal body protein; because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are usually not viable while heterozygous females show variable manifestations owing to X-inactivation. Impaired ciliary signalling in the kidney predisposes to cystic renal disease, and in the developing brain it contributes to callosal, cerebellar, and other midline malformations.
additionalDifferentials: Mohr syndrome (OFD type II) versus other OFD subtypes
Isolated cleft palate with limb anomaly
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dysmorphology and oral examination to document tongue, frenula, and palatal anomalies
Radiographs of the hands and feet to characterise digital malformations
Brain MRI for callosal, cerebellar, and posterior fossa anomalies including the molar tooth sign
Renal ultrasound to detect polycystic or cystic kidney disease
Molecular genetic testing including OFD1 and a ciliopathy gene panel
Developmental assessment where intellectual disability is present
redFlags: Progressive polycystic kidney disease leading to renal failure
Significant central nervous system malformation with neurological impairment or seizures
Airway or feeding compromise from severe oral and palatal malformation
Male fetal or neonatal loss suggesting an X-linked dominant lethal genotype
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype and organ involvement. Many females with type I have a normal or near-normal lifespan but may develop progressive polycystic kidney disease, while central nervous system malformation and severe systemic involvement worsen the outlook in some subtypes.
pitfalls: Classifying an affected child into the wrong OFD subtype and giving inaccurate prognostic and recurrence advice
Overlooking the ciliopathy association with progressive renal cystic disease requiring long-term surveillance
Missing subtle central nervous system malformation without dedicated brain imaging
Attributing oral hamartomas or extra frenula to isolated dental problems
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Surgically repair oral and craniofacial anomalies including cleft lip and palate closure, excision of tongue hamartomas and division of accessory frenula
Correct digital malformations such as syndactyly and polydactyly with orthopaedic and hand-surgery input
Provide longitudinal renal surveillance for cystic or polycystic kidney disease, managing hypertension with renin-angiotensin blockade and planning kidney replacement therapy as function declines
Offer neurodevelopmental support and manage associated CNS malformations, with early-intervention and educational services for intellectual disability
Coordinate dental and orthodontic care for dental anomalies and malocclusion
Involve a multidisciplinary craniofacial and clinical-genetics team
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given X-linked dominant (type I) inheritance, with molecular and prenatal testing where appropriate
